title: Every nation (Revelation 7:9–17)
hook: a great multitude of every nation and tongue, and God wipes away every tear

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four riders, and a cry from under the altar. Your line was how long? Which place did you stop and hold for a breath? Day one thousand three hundred.

John hears a number first. "An hundred and forty and four thousand," sealed from the tribes of Israel, twelve thousand from each tribe, named one by one. A careful count. Then he looks, and what he sees can't be counted at all. Two days ago he heard lion and saw lamb. Some readers notice the same move here: he hears a number, and sees a crowd too big for numbers. People from everywhere, standing in front of the throne in white, holding palm branches, all shouting at once. Today's word is who's in that crowd.

First, the crowd, in the King James words: "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands." Notice the list. Nations, kindreds, peoples, tongues. The text doesn't melt them into one. In heaven, by this picture, languages are still languages. And they cry together: "Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb." Second, who they are. An elder turns to John and asks: "What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they?" And John, who has seen so much already, says: "Sir, thou knowest." I don't know; you tell me. The elder answers: "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." Robes made white by washing them in blood. Christians read it as the Lamb's death making people clean. Third, the care. After yesterday's famine, this: "They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat." And the Lamb, the one who was slain, becomes their shepherd, and "shall lead them unto living fountains of waters." Fourth, the tears: "and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." It echoes Isaiah: "the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Wiping tears takes nearness. You can't do it from across a room; you have to be close enough to touch a face. Yesterday the question was how long. Today the answer isn't a date. It's a hand.

Here's the practice: picture a crowd of all nations. Settle, and breathe. Let faces come, slowly, from everywhere you can think of. Different skin, different clothes, different languages, all at once, and nobody asked to stop being who they are. Let in faces you know: a neighbor, a coworker, someone you've argued with. Let in faces you'll never meet. If you pray, you can join the crowd's own words: "Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb." If you don't, just stand among them for a while, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Every nation. John's great multitude that no one could number, from all nations, kindreds, peoples and tongues, fed and led by the Lamb, every tear wiped away.
Your line: every tear wiped. Today, notice one person carrying something heavy, and get close enough to ease it a little: a word, a coffee, an hour of your time. Day one thousand three hundred.

howItsDone: Revelation 7:9–17 is read at some Christian funerals and on All Saints' Day, as a picture of the saints from every nation gathered before God.

original.note: Greek: a nation, a people. the word behind 'nations' in Revelation 7:9.

trapdoor: what you thought: the crowd before the throne is one kind of people singing one kind of song.
what it means: a crowd no one can count, from all nations, kindreds, peoples and tongues, fed by the Lamb, every tear wiped.
what a scholar hears: John hears a counted number (7:4) and sees an uncountable crowd (7:9), and 7:17 echoes Isaiah 25:8.

notes: The 144,000 (7:4) and 'twelve thousand from each tribe' (7:5–8) are from the text. The script does not say who the 144,000 are; readings differ (Israel; the whole church; a literal number held by some groups). Confirm that leaving them uninterpreted is right.
'Some readers notice the same move' (hear a number, see a crowd; cf. hear lion, see lamb in 5:5–6) is attributed. Confirm.
'Christians read it as the Lamb's death making people clean' (7:14). Confirm wording.
howItsDone: use at some funerals and on All Saints' Day. Confirm.
